title: Aerospace Engineering
summary: Flight in air and in orbit. Lift is the first threshold (a wing turns airflow downward; the popular 'equal transit' story is false); the rocket equation is the second (every kilometre per second of Δv costs exponentially more propellant), and orbits run on intuitions that are often backwards.
sources: Curtis: Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students
Raymer: Aircraft Design: A Conceptual Approach

nodes.label: The Standard Atmosphere
nodes.summary: Pressure, density and temperature fall with altitude; density sets lift, drag and engine thrust.
nodes.outcome: Read density at altitude from the standard atmosphere.
nodes.check: Roughly how does air density at 11 km compare with sea level?
nodes.answer: About a third of the sea-level value (≈0.36 vs 1.225 kg/m³).

nodes.label: Lift
nodes.summary: L = ½ρv²SC_L. A wing turns the flow downward and the pressure difference that results lifts it; Newton and Bernoulli describe the same flow.
nodes.outcome: Compute lift and explain it with both pressure and momentum.
nodes.check: If an aircraft doubles its airspeed at the same angle of attack, how does lift change?
nodes.answer: It quadruples, since lift is proportional to v².

nodes.label: "Air over the top must meet the air underneath"
nodes.summary: The equal-transit-time explanation is false: air over the top arrives well before the air underneath.
nodes.outcome: Refute equal transit time with flow observations.
nodes.check: Do air parcels split at a wing's leading edge meet again at the trailing edge?
nodes.answer: No: the air over the top arrives well before the air underneath; the equal-transit explanation is false.

nodes.label: Drag & Lift-to-Drag Ratio
nodes.summary: Parasite drag grows with speed, induced drag falls with it; best L/D is where they are equal.
nodes.outcome: Find the speed for best glide from a drag polar.
nodes.check: A glider has L/D = 30. How far can it glide from 1 km up in still air?

nodes.label: Stall
nodes.summary: Past the critical angle of attack the flow separates and lift collapses.
nodes.outcome: Explain stall and recover from it.
nodes.check: What causes a wing to stall?
nodes.answer: Exceeding the critical angle of attack, so the flow separates from the upper surface and lift collapses.

nodes.label: "A stall happens below a certain speed"
nodes.summary: Stall is set by angle of attack, not speed; a hard pull-up can stall a wing at any speed.
nodes.check: Can a wing stall at high speed?
nodes.answer: Yes: stall depends on angle of attack, which a hard pull-up can exceed at any speed.

nodes.label: Stability & Control
nodes.summary: With the centre of gravity ahead of the neutral point, a pitch disturbance produces a restoring moment.
nodes.outcome: Check static stability from CG and neutral-point positions.
nodes.check: Why must an aircraft's centre of gravity be ahead of its neutral point?
nodes.answer: So a pitch disturbance produces a restoring moment: static stability.

nodes.label: Aircraft Performance & Range
nodes.summary: Climb, endurance and the Breguet range equation.
nodes.outcome: Estimate range with the Breguet equation.
nodes.check: By the Breguet range equation, what increases an aircraft's range?
nodes.answer: Higher lift-to-drag ratio, better engine efficiency (lower fuel consumption), and a larger fuel fraction.

nodes.label: Jet & Propeller Propulsion
nodes.summary: Thrust from accelerating air; propulsive efficiency favours moving lots of air slowly.
nodes.outcome: Compare turbojet, turbofan and propeller efficiency.
nodes.check: Why are high-bypass turbofans more fuel-efficient than turbojets?
nodes.answer: They accelerate a large mass of air by a little rather than a small mass by a lot, wasting less kinetic energy.

nodes.label: The Rocket Equation
nodes.summary: Δv = vₑ ln(m₀/m_f): velocity change grows only with the logarithm of the mass ratio, which is why rockets are mostly propellant and use stages.
nodes.outcome: Compute Δv and explain why staging helps.
nodes.check: A rocket with exhaust velocity 3 km/s and a mass ratio of e (≈2.72) can gain how much Δv?

nodes.label: Orbits as Free Fall
nodes.summary: An orbit is falling around the planet fast enough to keep missing it: v = √(GM/r) for a circle.
nodes.outcome: Compute circular orbital speed and period.
nodes.check: What speed keeps a satellite in a circular orbit 400 km up (r ≈ 6,771 km)?

nodes.label: "In orbit there is no gravity"
nodes.summary: Gravity at ISS altitude is about 90% of surface gravity; astronauts float because they are in free fall.
nodes.check: Gravity at the ISS's altitude is roughly what percentage of surface gravity?
nodes.answer: About 90%; astronauts float because they and the station are falling together.

nodes.label: Orbital Transfers
nodes.summary: The Hohmann transfer: two burns along an ellipse tangent to both orbits; the cheapest two-impulse transfer between nearby circles.
nodes.outcome: Compute Δv for a Hohmann transfer.
nodes.check: To move to a higher circular orbit with a Hohmann transfer, how many engine burns are needed?
nodes.answer: Two: one to enter the transfer ellipse and one to circularise at apoapsis.

nodes.label: "To catch a craft ahead, speed up"
nodes.summary: A prograde burn raises the orbit and lengthens the period, so you fall further behind; you drop lower to go round faster.
nodes.outcome: Plan a phasing manoeuvre to catch up with a target.
nodes.check: You are behind another spacecraft in the same orbit. Why doesn't a prograde burn help you catch it?
nodes.answer: It raises your orbit and lengthens your period, so you fall further behind; you must drop lower to go round faster.

nodes.label: Re-entry & Thermal Protection
nodes.summary: Orbital energy becomes heat; blunt bodies and ablators keep it off the vehicle.
nodes.outcome: Explain why blunt shapes survive re-entry.
nodes.check: Why do capsules re-enter blunt end first?
nodes.answer: A blunt shape makes a strong detached shock that keeps most of the heat in the air, away from the vehicle.

nodes.label: Flight Control Systems
nodes.outcome: Explain how fly-by-wire enables relaxed stability.
nodes.check: Why do fly-by-wire fighters use deliberately unstable airframes?
nodes.answer: Relaxed stability makes them more manoeuvrable; flight computers make constant corrections to keep them flyable.
